speechtext: On Motions.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ALLEGED ARRANGEMENTS FOR GOVERNMENT OFFICES IN GENEVA
speechtext:
On Friday the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) read an extract from the Mail and Empire concerning which I said I would make inquiry and give a further statement to-day. The item was as follows:
Canadian government has rented pretentious offices in the Quai Woodrow Wilson, where Dr. W. A. Riddell, permanent envoy, expects to entertain Canadians all summer.
Is this entertaining part of the policy of economy, or is it a correspondent's picturesque touch?
As a matter of fact, no premises have been rented in the Quai Woodrow Wilson. Premises have been rented in the Quai de Mont Blanc, not pretentious at all, at a rental of $500 a year. This will be reduced by sub-letting to $340 a year, or less than $30 a month. These rooms will be used for office purposes only, and are not intended in any way for entertaining.

The other afternoon the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) in his address in connection with this debate gave expression to these words:
That the financial statement given to the House does not reflect exactly and faithfully the conditions of the country at the present time, nor our financial standing.
With these words I entirely agree, in so far as they reflect my view in connection with this budget. In making this statement the hon. member intimated that perhaps his failure to interpret and understand properly the financial statement as presented by the Acting Finance minister (Mr. Robb) was attributable to his lack of expert knowledge of accountancy. Let me assure my hon. friend that such is not the case. I am prepared to assert, with a good deal of positiveness, that the more expert the accountant is who will examine into this statement as presented to the House, the more convinced he will be that it does not accurately reflect the condition of the country or correctly present the
existing state of public finances. As a matter of fact, it was a presentation that was hopeless in its confusion and baffling in its inaccuracies. This budget I icannot conceive as being other than deliberately designed to deceive the people as to the correct condition of affairs. It is a subtle expedient designed to shield a guilty and moribund government from the just indignation of an awakening public opinion.

speechtext:
Had I thought my right hon. friend would question my statement, I would have brought plenty of evidence in support of it. I have none under my hand at the moment, but I have no doubt of the accuracy of what I have stated. What are the impressions sought to be conveyed by this budget? The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) first assured the House that these accounts had been verified by two outside eminent chartered accountants. It is true he limited that verification of fact to certain things, but the impression that went forth to the public was that these accounts of the Dominion had been submitted to and approved by two outside, eminent chartered accountants. The next impression conveyed was that there was a surplus of $24,000,000, and some of my hon. friend's supporters are already claiming that such was the surplus. The third was that taxation had been reduced by $52,000,000, and the chief Liberal organ m the country the Globe, across the front page of its paper, the next day assured the taxpayers that there had been placed in their pockets by the government the enormous sum of $52,000,000. As regards the railways, there is an ominous silence, and I pause here to ask: Why, three months after the close of the railway fiscal year, we could not have had some accurate, definite, clear statement of the condition of our great railway investment. The next impression conveyed by the minister was that there was a favourable trade balance. Briefly, these statements summarize the impressions sought to be conveyed by the minister in his speech, and I purpose examining them at some length, step by step.
In the first place, let me examine the certificate of character which the minister presented to the House from the two eminent chartered accountants. I ask hon. members to listen to this certificate and to judge of its value. Personally, I assert before I read it that it is a perfectly meaningless and useless certificate. Will hon. members follow me for a moment while I read it? I shall not read what the minister said preceding it unless someone challenges me. I have the statement from the public accounts so that there will be no mistake about it. It is attached to the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada for the last fiscal year ended March 31, 1924. This is what the accountants said:
We have examined the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada as at March 31, 1924, and we certify that the balance sheet conforms to the balance sheets of previous years in not including in the net debt of the Dominion, issues of the Canadian National Railway company and companies included in its system, which carry the guarantee of the

Dominion of Canada. Such guaranteed issues are shown year by year as indirect liabilities.
Geo. Edwards,
Of the firm of Edwards, Morgan & Co.
W. Garth Thomson,
Of the firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. Ottawa, Canada, 27th January, 1925.
An absolutely meaningless, useless certificate -perfectly true!

speechtext:
I have great confidence
in chartered accountants, and I have such confidence in the two chartered accountants referred to that I am certain they would never give a certificate of approval to the accounts of this government as presented to the House. Now, what a mockery it is to say to an unemployed man with five children, "It is true, my friend, you cannot buy nourishing food for your children; it is true you cannot buy boots to put on your children's feet or clothing for their backs, but we have reduced taxation; we have put into your pocket $52,-
000.000. Why, we are a friend of yours. We have actually added to your resources as taxpayers $52,000,000." I say, Mr. Speaker, the thing is a mockery. What does this $52,000,000 consist of? What is the interpretation of it? In the first place I ask, have taxes been reduced? Is there one item of reduction in taxation? Has the sales tax been reduced? Has this onerous tax upon business, not upon individual incomes, but upon business in Canada, been reduced? Has the stamp tax, or the receipt tax, or any other tax been reduced? Not a nickel, not one cent. Not only have they not been reduced, but as a matter of fact business is being strangled, thousands are out of work, and 2,200 factories, large and small, in the last three years, with a magnitude of liabilities of $100,000,000, have gone to the wall. That is the condition.
Now let me examine this tax question for a moment. I have under my hand figures from the Customs and Excise department, and I find this; that in excise taxes, that is chiefly the sales tax, with a little from the stamp tax, but it does not include the taxes on liquor, which are kept separate-we will keep our mind on the sales tax, because this excise tax is chiefly made up of that-in 1923-1924 there was a collection of $115,000,000 of sales tax. This year there was a collection of $78,000,000, or a reduction of $37,000,000 and by the way that is in eleven months only. The minister made an estimate for the year, but I have given the actual figures for the eleven months ending with February and they show a. reduction of $37,000,000. If this is interpreted in the form of purchases, it means that there has been a falling off in purchases in Canada of $700,000,000. That is what it means. It simply means that business is not
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

being done. It does not matter what the government says to the public; it does not matter one iota how much they rebuke us for constantly calling attention to the condition of business; the stubborn fact is that there must have been a falling off in purchasing of $700,000,000. That is the interpretation of this saving of $52,000,000.
Now let me pass on to the income tax, of which I have particulars before me. I am not going to spend much time on it, but I want to show how we by our form and method of income taxation are militating against Canadian business men as compared with those against whom they are competing. I drew the attention of the House to this subject in the debate on the Address from the Throne, and I now have figures which I will give briefly because they are very illuminating. I will take the income tax of an individual doing business in Vancouver as against a man doing business in Seattle, and these figures are for personal income, not business income. On an income of $5,000 th<' Canadian would pay to the Dominion $126, and to British Columbia $95, or a total of $221. The man in Seattle would pay a tax of $50, or less than one-quarter of what his competitor in Vancouver has to pay. I bring it down to these intimate details so that we may appreciate more directly the onerous nature of this tax. I could go on down the list and give the income tax on incomes of $5,000, $6,000, $7,000, $8,000, $9,000, $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 and $25,000, but I shall take only a few to illustrate my point. The man in Vancouver or Canada with a salary of $7,000 pays in income tax a total of $493; the man in Seattle pays $100, or less than one-quarter, almost one-fifth. The man in Vancouver with an income of $10,000 pays $1,084; the man in Seattle pays $220. The point I want to make is this: We m Canada cannot expect to go on prospering and expanding in our business operations with the handicap of a tax of this kind. It is the application of this tax which I am asking the government to consider.
A moment ago I pointed out that a large number of firms had failed in business in Canada. On Friday last my hon. friend from Dufi'erin (Mr. Woods) made a statement in the House to which I wish to refer. I do not know whether he is in his seat; I think not, but he made this statement-Hansard page 1632:
I want to refer to a manufacturing concern in my own county. It is a woollen manufacturing industry and the only one we have in the county of Dufferin. That company to-day is running night and day shifts.
Mr. Caldwell:	I thought the woollen mills were
all shut down last year.

Mr. Woods:	There were rumours to that effect.
However the one in the county of Dufferin did not shut down but is running night and day shifts at the present time.
I thought that was strange, and I sought immediate and definite information. I have in my hand copies of wires received from Dods and Company, the firm referred to, in regard to this statement, and I shall read them, not because I want to embarrass the hon. member for Dufferin, but because I think it is well for us t.o face the facts. This ie from the secretary of the association:
Dods Knitting authorize me to inform you plant has not been operating night and day; that they are being forced to go on part time immediately. He is wiring explaining more fully.
Then I have this from Dods Knitting Company themselves:
Dods Knitting Company are not working day and night and are arranging to close to part time.

speechtext:
That is quite simple of
explanation, and I will tell my hon. friend exactly why it is. It is a very apt question he has asked. When we come to the end of a year and this applies with peculiar significance to the last session preceding an election-and I offer that merely as an indication of what we may look for in the future- it is the habit of any government to bring in all the resources it can, and show the highest realization on those resources, and at the same time to reduce their outstanding liabili-

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
ties all they can in order to make the best showing possible. In other words, towards the close of a year, a business firm will seek to collect in its debts, and put on a little pressure in collecting them, and probably take an inventory and reduce its stock as much as possible in order to make a good showing in its animal statement, for the year. Now what is the government doing this year? Business men all over the country know this, and they are reflecting upon it, that this government has during the past six months put on onerous pressure for the collection of income tax, a pressure that an many oases is embarrassing the person who is called upon to pay. We all have to pay, yes; but here is a situation that always arises in connection with the income tax, and nobody knows it better than my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). Very often the income tax is not assessed:-and this as the iniquity of the thing-for a year after it is incurred. Often tire assessment is delayed, not by the government, but by the machinery of government, and then suddenly the man is faced, at an inopportune moment with a tax of $5,000 or $10,000, or in the case of a large business it may run up into the hundreds of thousands, and he has not the money in hand or in the bank to immediately pay the tax. The government have been putting on pressure recently in collecting the income tax in order to make a Showing, in order to offset what they knew as far back as last October would be a fearfully alarming financial situation.

speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend mentions that; it will answer the question of my hon fiiend to the left (Mr. Beaubien). What we did prior to 1921 was this: Here was a firm known to be in an embarrassed condition, with charges amounting to $500,000 against them in the way of income tax and business profits tax. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) then Minister of Finance, or his predecessor, accepted a note. Why? For this reason: He could have pushed that business to the wall, shut it up and sold oui, its assets and collected what was due, because he had a prior charge. He said "No, we will allow them time to pay." That is somewhat different to what is going on at the present time. We were charged by no less an authority than the Prime Minister himself, and members of the present government, with having deliberately sought to defraud the people. That may not have been the Prime Minister's actual words, but that was the inference given to the country, and I believe it contributed very largely to the defeat of the then government. We were charged with having sought to defraud the taxpayer of his just due by accepting notes in lieu cf payment. What has the present government done? I want to know how long it took them to collect that note that they told us should have been paid and the payment of which they said should have been forced? I venture to say it was not paid for two years, and I do not know whether it has been paid yet or not. Why did they not on going into office at once collect that money? -because it was a demand note it was not a time note. Why did they not collect it? Because the judgment of the Prime Minister, the judgment of the Minister of Railways, the judgment of the Acting Minister of Finance, and the judgment of the Minister of Justice was that it would be unwise to force that company to the wall in order to collect that tax,
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

and therefore by their action they put the stamp of approval on the policy of their predecessors. That is an answer to my hon. friend's (Mr. Beaubien) question as to the policy and the action of the previous government.
Now 1 turn to the subject of Trade and Commerce and come to the claim of the Acting Minister of Finance that the exports showed a favourable balance over imports of
8263,000,000. First, I want to ask the Acting Minister of Finance why he did not bring down particulars of the Australian treaty in his budget? 1 am going to venture a guess as to why he did not and it will be interesting, I think, to my hon. friends to my left. If that Australian treaty had been brought down and had showed some increases in the tariff-which we asked for and which we were anxious to see in it; we approve of it-it might have antagonized hon. members to my left. So the government said "No. Let us separate these matters. Let us confuse the Progressives. We will deal with the dumping clause in the budget and the Progressives will not be unduly alarmed. And we will bring down the Australian treaty separately. Although the Progressives may oppose it the Conservatives will support it, and so we will escape the vote of the combined opposition." But the budget ought to have contained the provisions of the Australian treaty, which treaty was concluded seme months ago.
Now let me turn to an examination of the trade situation. The Acting Minister of Finance claims that there is a favourable balance of trade of $263,000,000. This sounds very well but I want to study the claim for a moment. I contend that we ought to look at our national business just as strictly as a private firm will scrutinize its business. What are the facts? In the first place I ask, is this favourable balance an actual balance, and what does it mean to Canada? I intend to examine it at some length in order to get a proper appreciation of the value of this supposed excess of exports over imports. We must remember that Canada is a very heavy borrowing country. We have borrowed from the United States upwards of two billion and a half dollars; we have borrowed from Great Britain upwards of two billion and a half dollars. The best authorities in the world fix the borrowings in each case at a higher sum than two and a half billion dollars. In addition we have borrowed from France and from one or two other countries as well, but I am leaving the smaller borrowings out and wish to focus attention for the moment on the large borrowings. Now when a nation borrows what

is the import of it to that country? How is interest on the borrowing paid? It is paid in two ways: First it is paid by exports; secondly if the amount is not covered by exports then it is added to the debt of the country. Now here are some figures that are somewhat interesting. Our accounts with the United States and with Great Britain show about as follows: The Acting Minister of Finance told the House that we had $263,000,000 to the good, and hon. members all around him thumped their desks in ecstasy. But what is the actual situation? Here are the figures which strikingly illustrate it: The interest to the United States on investments in Canada, amounting to $2,500,000,000, at the rate of 6 per cent is $150,000,000 a year. A great many of these investments carry a much higher rate of interest. There are industrials paying 10 or 12 per cent; some of them pay very much higher than six and very few of them less than six; some of them pay 5i per cent. I think our Dominion loans amount to only about $700,000,000, carrying about 5 per cent, so that I am well within the mark in my interest calculations. We owe' the United States at the end of each year $150,000,000 of interest and we owed her last year on our trade transactions $159,000,000 or a total of $309,000,000 that we were to the bad in our transactions with the United States for last year. How was that paid? It was paid by simply increasing the mortgage hold of the United States on Canada. Whether it was by industrials or by financial concerns it does not matter; it means that the people of the United States have that much more hold upon Canada. In other words it reflects exactly what has happened in the last ten years-I think I should say more correctly twelve or fourteen years-our borrowings from the United States, or our indebtedness to that country, have increased from less than 1,000,000,000 to $2,500,000,000. So we went behind in our dealings with the United States last year to the extent of $309,000,000. Our account with Great Britain stands as follows: Great Britain owed us on trade $242,900,000 but we owed her $150,000,000 interest. If we deduct the interest that leaves $92,000,000. If we deduct the $92,000,000 from the $309,000,000 it shows that as a nation, as a business entity, as a corporate body we were $216,000,000 to the bad last year in our external business. And I want to point out that our dealings *with other countries do not any more than offset our interest debt to them, and one will cancel the other. Now, if this is the state of affairs we ought to ask ourselves the question "Is the fiscal policy of this country of a char-

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
acter that is leading Canada into prosperity, or are we piling up and adding to our obligations to a point where there may be danger? Let me illustrate the case a little differently. Last year the balance of trade with the United States against us was the smallest it has been,
I think, for perhaps fifteen years or more. If we take the average for sixteen years it will give us a better idea. The average adverse balance of trade with the United States for the last sixteen years is $223,000,000 per annum. Add that to the sum of $150,000,000 for interest and we find that we are going behind with the United States to the extent of $375,000,000 per annum, and the ratio is increasing because each year our interest debt is increasing. This is a serious situation and we have to face it.
Where are we drifting in this fiscal policy? Where are we drifting in our transactions with the other countries of the world? How long can we stand it? I gave a simple illustration not long ago, and I will repeat it now. A man has a farm or a small business. He has something he owns out of which he is getting a living, perhaps a very decent living. He wants to expand a little. He borrows five hundred dollars and gives a mortgage on his farm. The next year he wants an automobile and borrows one or two thousand dollars and adds that to the mortgage on his farm. It is true the five hundred and the thousand dollars, or the two thousand whatever it is, does not bother him much because his farm is worth it, but if he goes on year after year adding to the mortgage, the time will come when there will be a foreclosure, and those who have been lending him the money will say:	"We
want to cash in on this deal". The question is how long can Canada continue increasing its indebtedness abroad without embarrassing the economic life of the country. That is the question facing Canada. Whither are we drifting? It is true Great Britain and Greece, for fifty years or more have had an excess of imports over exports, and these cases have been cited as an'answer to the argument I am presenting. But it must be borne in mind that Great Britain had an invisible revenue before the war, and still has a revenue now of perhaps four hundred million pounds per annum in shipping revenue. She goes out into the markets of the world, carries other people's goods, and obtains a large revenue from it. That is part of the excess of the imports. It is debts being paid to her. We owe her a hundred and fifty million dollars a year. How do we pay it? We send over grain or manufactured goods or whatever we can sell to her. For the last half century or century
or perhaps two centuries Britain has been collecting revenue from all corners of the world, and it comes in in the form of imports; consequently she can stand an excess of imports over exports. But we cannot because we are not a loaning country. We are a borrowing country. The same thing applies to Greece as to Great Britain. The chief revenue of Greece is in the form of tourist traffic, and this traffic leaves considerable money in the country. We have no such sources of revenue. We have some tourists coming into the country, and I am glad to see that the number is increasing, and I think the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) should keep his eye on the tourist traffic, in order to help the country pay its debts; but the revenue derived from that traffic will not be sufficient to meet the three hundred and seventy five million a year. That is the point we have to keep in mind.
The time will come in the history of all debts and all mortgages when the stage of foreclosure is reached. I am not saying that the point of foreclosure is reached in Canada. I say, speaking perhaps now for myself-and every hon. gentleman can take it as he likes- I would consider myself a little less than a madman if I waited until the point of foreclosure came before raising my voice in opposition to this policy of drifting which is in vogue in the country now. I would consider we were traitors to the country if we understood the problem, appreciated the danger and allowed the drifting to go on until we approximately reached the point of foreclosure. I do not think that point has been reached, but I say the evidence of increasing obligations abroad is such that every sensible man and woman in the country is called upon to face the problem. Whatever the remedy may be, let everyone face the situation and acknowledge its difficulties.
I desire to say a few words in regard to some of the resolutions. I have something to say in regard to the dumping clause, but I notice that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), recognizing that discretion is the better part of valour, decided to retreat hastily from the position assumed on the introduction of the budget in regard to the dumping clause. It reminds us of a budget introduced three years ago. If I recollect correctly, there were three distinct budgets- two absolutely distinct budget speeches in the one year. I wonder if we are to expect any further injection of new matter into the budget before a vote is taken. I think the minister, or whoever was responsible for devising these items, should have known be-
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

fore they introduced the resolution what they know now, and I think did know it. But the minister thought he could throw this sop out to some people other than my hon. friends to my left, and win a little support from them; but when he was greeted with the evident anger and indignation of my hon. friends to my left he thought perhaps he would not gain as much as he would lose. I think that is the secret of the whole story.
Regarding the export of power, I am not going to deal with the question in any detail. I shall reserve that till the resolution is in committee. But this resolution vertually establishes the principle of the export of power, and this is the point I want to bring to the attention of the House. This method of dealing with power and this public enunciation of the intention to increase revenue out of the export of power virtually establishes the principle or policy of the export of power, and further it will develop a vested right that will be mightily embarrassing in a few years to come. Then we have the fact that we have been exporting pulpwood. We have business men on the other side of the line going to the United States congress and government and demanding that the government of the United States shall put a heavy hand on the government of Canada to prevent us taking any action we wish to take. Why? Because they say that they have established mills depending on this resource, and have established a vested right which they say should be respected. I am not going to debate that question, but if this resolution carries as it stands now, it will be tantamount to a declaration to the public that we are going into the business of exporting power and will open the way to the establishment of a vested right that will be international in character.
That is not all. I desire to bring this to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), under whose department this matter falls, although he is not in his seat just now. Power is not a product. It is a tool. You might just as well take the machinery out of some of your factories and ship it to the other side, as to export your power to the United States. I want to emphasize if I can the point that power is not a product but a tool. It is a tool with which we can accomplish things in the way of industrial development in this country. It is not a product in itself, and it should not be viewed as a product or as a commodity to export. It should be carefully guarded as a useful implement for Canadians. I am not saying that we should immediately cut off the per-

mission to sell export power, but if any of it is to be exported, it should be done on the basis that if we have any excess that we are not using, we will lend this power or this tool or this implement, under license for a year, to the people on the other side, but we should not part with the control or the vested right in that resource. If this resolution passes it will fix a definite limitation to the extension of Canadian industry. I pause to emphasize that point and I want to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, and the attention of your colleagues from Quebec, to the fact that it will affect that province more than it will affect any other section of Canada. And it will affect my own province. And why? In Quebec, and I take it in all the provinces outside of Ontario, power is in private hands. Once the principle is adopted and the vested interest is established, private interests will so develop for their own selfish ends the export of this power that the time will come when others in Canada desiring to use it will find that the point of limitation has been reached. I repeat to my hon. friend-and it is the duty of every hon. member to recognize and realize this-that it will fix the limitation of expansion of industry in Canada, and it is nothing more nor less than placing a noose around the neck of Canadian industry with United States capitalists on the free end of the rope, so that at any moment suitable to them the noose can be tightened and Canadian industry strangled. This may seem like strong language, but sometimes it takes strong language to offset the persistent intention and determination of a government to dissipate our heritage.

I have tried to make this clear to my hon. friend. I may have been a little obtuse in my reasoning, and if my hon. friend has not understood it, that is my fault. If this resolution passes, it virtually means that Canada publicly admits that she is to follow a policy of the sale of power as a product. I point out to the House that power should not be looked upon as a product for sale at all ; that power is a tool, or a weapon, or an implement, if you like, in the hands of manufacturers for purposes of production. It is not in itself a product. If we establish a system of export upon a revenue basis, that

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
is upon the principle of producing revenue to the country, we shall establish vested rights on the other side of the line. Indeed, those rights are there now; they are raising their heads to-day, even though we have been exporting power only under license. There is a vast difference between the two-establishing the sale of power as a product, and merely lending it, as I said a moment ago, under a yearly license. My other criticisms have have been criticisms of the proposed policy cf the government. I say this to the government, not in criticism, their present policy *.'light to be surveyed; we ought to look carefully into our license system of the present day and determine whether or not we should make it more clear than we have that any power we part with is simply as an act of grace for the time being. As a matter of fact, this is what this House should say: That we do not purpose permitting the continuance of the export of power. I do not say that we should cut off the export of power at a moment's notice.

speechtext: I do not wish to criticize in the least. It is only for information I am asking this question. There has been a great deal of dispute amongst scientific men and deep thinkers about the export of power because we cannot cancel contracts that we make with the United States. If we are permitted to impose an export duty of $1.95 per horse power per annum, is there anything to hinder this parliament from making it $20 per horse power?

speechtext:
Nothing in the world. I think I understand what my hon. friend has in mind. Recognizing that certain contracts have been entered into and appreciating, as we must, the moral value or ethics of good faith, let us cany out those contracts or permit the carrying out of them, but let us make clear to the public that it is not a policy we are adopting. Let the United States know that they are not going to build up industries over there under Canadian hydroelectric power. That is my contention.
I may be asked what suggestions I have to make, because I appreciate that if I spend nearly an hour, as I have, in offering criticisms, somewhat sharp, of the government, it is up to me to offer some constructive suggestions, and I shall do so. If I had anything to do with the matter. I would make these suggestions:
1.	To switch some of our purchases from the United States to other sources and change an adverse balance of trade of some $223,000,000 per annum to a favourable one sufficient
to meet our annual interest indebtedness to that country. There are two ways by which this adverse balance of trade can be changed. One is for the United States to increase her purchases from us and the other is for us to decrease our purchases from them. As I have stated on other occasions, the United States will understand the language of "dollars and cents" more quickly than anything else, and if we want our friends south of the line to appreciate the customer they have north of the line, the best way is to withdraw sonjje business from them.
2.	To encourage the investment of Canadian capital in industry by removing irritating and overburdensome types of taxation; by adjusting the tariff so as to direct our vast reserves of raw materials to use in Canadian factories, and by tax or embargo to discourage the reckless export of raw materials and make abundantly clear that Canadian power is to remain under control for Canadian industry.
3.	Recognizing that Great Britain has for decades been our best customer, to adopt such an attitude towards the Motherland and sister dominions as will lead to closer cooperation within the empire in trade matters, and to avoid scrupulously all appearances of discord in relation to foreign affairs.
In conclusion, this budget is a delusion and a snare. It does not disclose the full extent of the nation's obligations and commitments; nor does it correctly interpret the revenue accounts of the country; nor does it show either the real value of costliness of our $2,000,000,000 railway investment. It gives us no syllable of information on that, nor does ii give any adequate idea of the condition of our internal trade, as I think I have well shown. But, on the contrary, it deceives the public as to the public debt. It mocks the taxpayer as to his taxes. It seeks to bury all of this under a meaningless certificate from two eminent outside accountants. The minister offers in answer to this: "Remember our great heritage." I have his full statement, but he calls on us to remember our great heritage. Where do this government stand? Do they favour free trade? Then, let them say so. Do they intend to protect Canadian industry? If so, let them stop pussy-footing and cease tolling the "death knell of protection." I understand the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) may do me the honour of following me. If he does, I am going to listen very carefully for that "death knell of protection."

speechtext:
I ask this question: Do
the government favour making Canada an economic adjunct of the United States? If so, then let them come out into the open and declare themselves frankly. Let them say that Canadian power, jCanadian resources, Canadian copper, Canadian pulpwood, Canadian nickel, Canadian asbestos are to be produced for the purpose of feeding the manufactories of the United States.
If it is not their policy let them face the fact that this condition exists and let them attempt to put an end to this drift which is undoubtedly making of this country a mere economic adjunct to the United States. If the government is concerned about this tendency'' and are anxious to arrest it let them face squarely the $309,000,000 of a deficit in our dealings with the United States and let them tell us what they intend to do to rectify that condition of things. The economic and social conditions in Canada to-day demand definite action. The people are sick and tired of the policy of drift and are anxious to see this country economically sound. Everyone knows that Canada has a great heritage and there was no necessity whatever for the minister to mote that fact in his budget. speech. But what is required is a proper administration of that heritage; what is required is effective management by the government of the heritage that has been placed in their hands as a trust. That heritage the Canadian people desire to see developed in the interests of this country and not in exploitation and spoliation by aliens. This government stands charged before the .people of the country with crass indifference to its own pledges; with ruthless dissipation of our resources; with duplicity in policy and with utter disregard of governmental responsibility. And it stands 
charged further with administrative practices which will end in delivering Canada economically bound and shackled to the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. SNOWBALL (Northumberland, N. B.):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OP THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I regret the evident disappointment of the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) at not being followed by a minister of the crown. In this instance, however, the government has chosen a back bencher to reply to the hon. member and I am pleased to have this opportunity of following so able a gentleman as my hon. friend who was an administrator in the government of which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) was head.
I wish at the outset to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on. the agreeable surprise he sprang on his Liberal followers by being able to show an actual credit balance for the year ending March 31, 1925, of $1,823,000. We need not for the moment take into consideration the
34,000,162, which might be subject to some criticism. The achievement is a creditable one without this item. I also wish to congratulate ham on the bomb he thus throws into the Conservative comer. It was amusing.. Mr. Speaker, to see the falling countenances that followed this declaration, as they were in anticipation of the opportunity of enjoying a substantial deficit.
In view of the trade conditions that prevailed in the early .part of 1924 that warranted a revival of trade in "free trade England" and alike in "high protection United States," it was certainly a great disappointment to all business men to find that better conditions did not materialize but that in both countries, exemplifying the two opposing trade policies, similar conditions prevailed, that trade languished and unemployment was intensified.
It was therefore, Mr. Speaker, all the more to the credit of the acting minister and the Liberal administration, that they were able after having freed the Canadian people of a substantial burden of taxation by the reduced tariff last session, to accomplish what many large business concerns were unable to do- show a balance.
The hon. member (Mr. Stevens) implied that there were apparently no reductions this year of any account, or at any rate no reductions that would lead to any saving to the Canadian people. But the hon. gentleman overlooks a large number of items in connection with which the tariff has been reduced. For instance, the list includes mowing machines, cultivators and farm imple-

The Budget-Mr. Snowball
merits of different kinds as well as farm wagons; while reductions have been made on fertilizers. There are also reductions in the case of spraying machines, incubators for hatching eggs, brooders for young fowls, milking machines, and so on; and rock drills, saw mills, logging machinery and logging wagons are reduced. We find too that the sales tax is reduced on rubber boots from 6 per cent to 2i per cent and it is proposed to remove the sales tax on cereals, while there is a reduction from 6 per cent to 2| per cent on canned vegetables, canned fruits, jams and things of that kind. Ail along the line reductions have been made, thus removing a considerable burden from the shoulders of the people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, reverting to the Roumanian and Greece interest payment, I consider the acting minister deserves the commendation of this House for his efforts in more fully providing, not only protection for the original debts, contracted by our Conservative friends when in power, but for the inclusion in this, security of the arrear interest. Would any business man tell the House where he would put the four million dollars interest item, except as placed by the financial statement? The interest paid on this money borrowed for this loan has been a debit item each year, and included in interest payment, and when a payment is made in cash, or security, it surely would go to credit of interest account. True, it is not actually paid in cash, but it stands a secured payment on interest to debit of Roumania, Greece and a credit to interest account-and not a capital sum. The security now is bonds with coupons attached. I believe, and members on the other side of the House have admitted, that it will now be paid.
In general business we would treat an adequately secured account in that way especially when they were paying interest regularly and would be justified in so doing. Now my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) refers to the Home Bank case, and almost by implication wishes to leave the impression that the hon. the Acting Minister of Finance may eventually do time. But, Mr. Speaker, the circumstances are different, and I hope the acting minister is not losing any sleep. The Home Bank accounts on which interest was charged and credited to show favourable balances were hopeless, admittedly so, by even the bank officials, and proven so by actual results-no interest paid for years -but in this case the hon. member for West York says, " I am inclined to think they are going to come through ". And he has every
reason to be pleased that such a reckless expenditure by his government has been so favourably placed through the vigilance of the Liberal administration. Quite a frank admission the above, and practically justifying as far as he could the action of the acting minister. In fact since 1922, or since this government has been in power, the interest has been regularly paid.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us touch for a moment on the railway situation; and at the outset I wish to state that I am fully in sympathy with the suggestion made by the hon. leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke), that the railways be re-valued and written down to actual valuation. But again there are difficulties, and after you have done so, then what? Have you changed the situation any as far as Canada is concerned? liability, but in one instance it is a direct liability, and the other an indirect, with an increasing physical value as our trade under Liberal regime improves. At present, with a direct liability of $2,417,000,000, is it wise to make any change?

I wish now for the edification of the official opposition to read further from the speech of the hon. member for Dufferin. The extract is not very long, but shows what did take place within that party:
That was in 1910. The Conservative policy then was, "We must get down to a lower tariff". They were going to appeal to the people and wanted to get hold of the people on that low tariff policy. But what happened? The Liberals outwitted them, went over to the United States and stole the Conservative platform. We know that the Conservative policy back in the eighties and nineties was that as soon as the United States was willing to put the natural products of the country on the free list Canada would do the same, and that we would have reciprocity in the natural products of the country. But the United States refused to accede to that request until 1911, when the Liberals went over there and made an arrangement with them in regard to it. The Conservatives then felt that they were up against it, that the Liberals had taken tlie ground under their feet, and some scheme had to be launched. What were they to do? They wanted to get into power. At that particular time I knew a little of the workings of that historic party to my right, and I got into the caucus. I have not time to tell my hon. friends about it to-night, because I have to catch the train.
I am extremely sorry, Mr. Speaker, he had to catch a train, because I would like him to have unfolded to us all the doings of that caucus, which launched the flag-waving scheme of 1911. He goes on:	.
They said, "There is one hope of getting into power, and that is the loyalty cry". They raised the Union Jack to the top of the mast. I do not know what they did in other localities, but I know that in my locality they fought the contest on that particular line and nothing else, and they succeeded in winning.
We can see by these statements, Mr. Speaker, which are made by one who was in close touch with the party at that time, that the Conservatives were not sincere in their attitude towards reciprocity, but were willing at any time to sacrifice the interests of Canada in order to secure power and get on the treasury benches of Canada.
We in the Maritime provinces are against high tariffs. We would ask the government to seriously consider further reductions. I realize that we cannot make any radical changes, but I would ask the government to give notice to the manufacturers that we cannot afford always to have them as cripples on crutches, and that they should try and

take, a few steps without artificial support until they nan eventually throw their crutches away. We do not want to be inhuman and ruthlessly kick them from underneath them, but we would advise them to take warning, improve their methods, if necessary, cut down their property values, and prepare for what may come in the very near future.
Trade is improving in this country, and to-day we are in a more sound and healthy condition than the country to the south. Every bank president in the country has sounded a hopeful note in his presidential address before the annual meeting, but at the same time every one of them has advised caution and economy, and we realize that is good advice, and the practice of both by government and people alike will the more quickly bring about a sound financial basis for this country.
Now I wish to read to the House some clippings I have recently taken from the Daily Telegraph-Journal, St. John, N.B.,-a paper that has done much to interest the rest of Canada in the Maritimes-another dated February 19, from the Citizen, and a third from a Conservative paper published in Fredericton, the Daily Gleaner, under date March 27. The clipping from the Daily Telegraph-Journal says:
Cotton Mills on Full Time Again
Cornwall and York now working six days a week
"Back again to full time" was the cheering news that about 400 employees of the Cornwall and York cotton mills received early this week after 18 months of curtailed operations. The change is effective at once so that instead of closing down yesterday as usual for the rest of the week the mills will operate until Saturday noon as they do under normal conditions.
Market is Better
An improvement in the cotton market and the securing of some additional contracts by the local mills, it was learned on good authority yesterday, have brought about the resumption of full time. While it is not definitely known for how long a period this will continue efforts will be made to keep the mills on full time during the next few months.
The congestion of the market more than a year and a half ago hit all the cotton mills throughout the country hard and in many cases they shut down altogether for a time. The local mills have been operating on part time during this period of depression. Lately both the Cornwall and York mills have been running four days a week.
Improves Conditions
Employees of the mills and their families greeted the return to full time, with the corresponding increase in the size of their pay envelopes, with relief. Struggling along as best they could with only part time at the mills and with the high cost of necessities it has been a time of hardship for many. Landlords, store keepers etc. in the vicinity of the mills will also benefit by the return to normal conditions. In fact the effect of the increased work will make itself felt more or less throughout the city, a citizen pointed out yesterday, and will help greatly in restoring better times around St. John.

The clipping from the Citizen reads: Hardware Trade on Sound Footing President of Sheet Metal Company Prophesies Bright Business Future
Toronto, Feb. 19.-Business has reached a sound footing, which will enable advance purchases and bring about business stability. T. A. Enslow, president of a sheet metal plant of Hamilton, told the Retail Hardware Merchants' Association here yesterday.
Canada was facing a steadily brightening outlook, he said, and retailers could look ahead for several months at prevailing prices.
Speaking in a broader sense, Mr. Enslow declared that Canada should go slow in the matter of immigration, for with the steady increase of "good times" there not only would be a return of the thousands of Canadians, who had crossed the border to the United States, but these would bring with them many Americans to become Canadians.
I find the following in the Gleaner with respect to loans:
Loans well met in the Maritimes Plenty of money available and interest rates to be lower.
St. John, N. B., March 27.-George H. Smith, of Toronto, General Manager of the Canada Permanent Mortgage Corporation and the Canada Permanent Trust Company, while here to-day, suggested that the local Boards of Trade invite members of the Toronto, Montreal and western boards of trade to come to the Maritimes and study conditions at first hand.
Mr. Smith said that all over Canada there was the dawn of better times and there was much more hopeful feeling among the business men. He predicted cheaper money for industry and a plentiful supply. All that was needed now for real prosperity was population and an additional half million people would make the wheels of industry hum.
Mr. Smith said his company had over $3,000,000 invested in mortgage loans in the Maritime provinces and they were extremely gratified at the way payments [DOT] had been met on both principal and interest. In no part of the Dominion had payments been better.
In the western provinces conditions were on the mend.
As to the whole situation, he said a person would be a great deal of a pessimist who could not see the prospect of real improvement.
Mr. Smith will sail to-day on the Montcalm to spend a couple of months in England, where he will make arrangements for a supply of English capital for Canada.
He could assure the Maritime province industries that plenty of money would be available on mortgage loans and that the interest rates were bound to be lower.
Let us give up our pessimistic whining attitude, throw back our shoulders, and go forward hopefully into the future. We in this parliament can injure Canada by our unwise utterances in this House, or we can help smooth the path towards prosperity. Which attitude are we going to take?
I was going to make some reference to the dumping clause, but I find the Acting Minister of Finance has made a change in the clause of which I am a little doubtful as to whether it was really in the interest of Canada or not. I want, however, to refer to the fact that there was a saving to Canada under the duties that
we have had. I referred to that earlier in my remarks in reply to certain hon. members from the west. I showed the changes that had been made and pointed out that there was an actual saving to the people of Canada both in customs duties and in sales tax. There may have been some shrinkage of business but it does not represent a very large amount. The actual figures are obtainable and will show that notwithstanding this shrinkage there was a very large saving to the people through the reduction made in taxes. It may not have been as large as was anticipated at the time owing to the fact that we had a reduced trade this year which was not expected when the estimate was made to parliament of what the return would likely be. Still the saving is large and the people have benefited beyond all doubt from the policy pursued by the government. I am sure because of the government's record the people wdll have confidence in it just as they had in 1921; and wdienever the present government decides to go to the country the public confidence in it will be shown by the substantial vote that will be recorded for the Liberal party all over Canada.
In conclusion I come to the consideration of a matter that was discussed more than any other during my recent campaign by my opponents who thought they enjoyed a monopoly of it and rang the changes on it just as they did in the case of the flag-waving cry of 1911. I refer to what has been wrongly termed "Maritime rights". I am in no sympathy with any such name being applied to our problems. We have no rights as such. We are part of a great Dominion and we have problems to overcome. But every province has problems, and our problems like the others are such as each of us can help the other to solve. We looked for great results to come from the Intercolonial railway. The space between Upper and Lower Canada was to be bridged, and it was expected that a flow of merchandise -our fish, our lumber, our produce-would go west and the manufactures of the west would come east. In one particular the expectation was fulfilled. The manufactures came east, but our goods had to go in the same old way to the markets of Europe and the United States. However the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) went fully into this and I need not discuss it.

Our great industries are certainly discriminated against. Do you not agree, Mr. Speaker, that we have just cause for complaint and that the other provinces should insist on such an unjust handicap being removed. We must have lower freight rates and passenger rates if we are going to make this country of ours grow. We cannot under the conditions as they exist at the present time 
develop industries or develop trade within Canada unless a very substantial reduction is made in our freight rates, and I trust such legislation will be brought in at the present session of parliament as will make it possible to bring about the equitable rates so necessary to develop trade not only in the Maritime provinces but in the western provinces as well. We are looking for such legislation and I hope it will be available at the present session of parliament. We have our winter ports, St. John and Halifax, and rve were pleased to find that the action of the government in limiting the British preference to goods passing through Canadian ports had [DOT] resulted in only a fraction of one per cent coming in otherwise, but we feel that every Canadian National employee should be a booster for Canada and Canadian ports, and should use his influence to have these Maritime ports used in the winter. Spend money on our harbour facilities, spend money on making the entrance to them safe, spend money on breakwaters or anything that will increase trade. Do not economize on matters of this kind as it would be false economy and would tend to retard the growth of our country. With reference to immigration, we have been very much neglected in this particular, the railways desiring the long haul. I would ask the government to be very careful in regard to the selection. Do not bring industrial workers to the industrial centres until industrial workers who are there now have been absorbed by the increase in industry which is sure to take place in the coming year. We can use the right kind of farmers in New7 Brunswick. We have many vacant farms which became vacant during the period between 1878 and 1896. We have farm lands that are available for these settlers, adjacent to the cities, towns and villages. We would ask the government, in considering their immigration policy, not to pass by the Maritime provinces, but to bring the immigrants into New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. We have to import too much farm produce in our province. We have good land and good opportunity, and we invite the government so to frame their immigration policy that they will bring to the Maritime provinces the number of people necessary for the upbuilding of eastern Canada. We need them as much as they do in the west. As Canada is built up m population, as we increase the number of people in the country, by the better class of people of our own

The Budget-Mr. Snowball
nationality, people from the British Isles as far as we can, we will be doing one of the best things we can do for the country. If five hundred or a thousand people are brought into these provinces you will find a difference in the trade and in the outlook. We are a responsible people down there, and we will be able to show these newcomers that we have a country equally as good as Ontario or Quebec or the great northwest. These people will realize that the Maritime provinces will give them homes and encourage others to come. The difficulty is that people have never come our way. The great northwest has loomed up big and many people have gone in that direction. I ask the government to take notice of this and have the Immigration department look into the matter. Some effort should be made to bring into this country the people we need to fill up our farms and our country to make our Maritime provinces what we consider they should be.
Men have been brought from the north of Scotland trained in the fishing industry and they were taken out into the western country where they will not see a halibut or a salmon.
Mjr hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) spoke of the fish on the Great Lakes, and in the vicinity of Manitoba. If those men were brought to New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, and went into the counties on the sea shore, they would find a condition similar to what they had left, employment they were accustomed to, and they would have the bracing sea air that they will miss in the west.
Finally we have another railway problem in New Brunswick which I would like to bring to the attention of the government. Branch lines were taken over in New Brunswick in 1904, 1906, 1917, 1920 and 1922, and are a paying part of the Canadian National system. I say a paying part, because I have it on the best authority that some of the branch lines I know about are a creditable asset to the Canadian National Railways, and are producing a revenue better than that produced by many of the other parts of the railway in Canada.
I would like to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to this matter, and I would like him to take into consideration that the government of New Brunswick gave bonds to the promoters. While in other provinces they guaranteed the bonds and the guarantee bonds are now assumed by the Dominion and New Brunswick contributes its share. The amount 107

These railways are a paying part of the Canadian National Railways. I think the New Brunswick government should be recouped, the bonds in connection with these railways should be taken off their hands and they should be placed in exactly the same position as the other provinces in connection with the transfer of railways. I think that is a fair proposition, and should appeal to every hon. member in this chamber, whether Liberal, Conservative or Progressive. All that we ask is that we be dealt with fairly, in the same way as the provinces of Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta were dealt with, and that the money advanced to the railways should be taken off the shoulders of the New Brunswick government and become a part and parcel of the indebtedness of the great National railway system. We have assumed our part and portion of these other guaranteed bonds. We are a part of Canada. Assuming that, I think we have every right to ask the government of this country to treat the Maritime provinces exactly as the other provinces have been treated, and we feel that our province should be relieved, as other provinces were relieved, of this responsibility.
Then we have the Valley railway, operated as a part of the Canadian National and under lease, having cost the province $7,111,977 for about 180 miles, or about $40,000 per mile. This line was built on the same standard as the National Transcontinental. It is now leased to the Canadian National, and I say this line should be taken over by the Canadian National Railways, and that the Canadian National should assume the liability of the province of New Brunswick. There is nothing unreasonable in this request. I know that this is a large order. I know that the government of the province of New Brunswick is not responsible for the condition as it exists at the present time, but that railway 'is hampering the growth and freedom of the people of the Maritime provinces, because they have not sufficient means within the province or available with which to raise revenue and pay interest on an investment of that nature. The government, having taken over

The Budget-Mr. Snowball
COMMONS [DOT]
the other branch lines, I think could very well afford to take over this line, even with the large investment in railways, which was stated by one hon. member to be $1,800,000,000 It would enable the province to invest money which would then be available to them, for other works in the province. We have been considering the question of the water powers in the province of New Brunswick, and if these railways were taken off our hands it would make it possible for our people to develop the water-powers, having been relieved of these interest rates in connection with this railway enterprise.
I bring this to the attention of the government and I hope they will consider the matter. I think hon. members coming from the Maritime provinces, and members from the other provinces will agree that in all fairness the province of New Brunswick should be assisted in this way, and it would only be carrying out the understanding which was arrived at when the province came into confederation. Now is the time when the government can hold out the olive branch and say, "We are prepared to relieve you of your obligations in connection with the railways, as we did with the other provinces, and we know that the province will then prosper".
The Kingsclear branch bill was thrown out by the Senate last year. We hope that it will again pass the House and be favourably considered in the Senate. We need this branch. It will shorten the haul from northern New Brunswick to Boston points, some 350 miles. It will be the connecting link that will make the Valley railway a paying piece of road and it will encourage the establishment of industry along the Canadian National.
Another line of railway that we hope the government will seriously consider-and it has been brought before Sir Henry Thornton who looks upon it with favour-is the extension of what is known as the Caraquet and Gulf Shore road from Tracadie along towards Newcastle, a distance of about sixty miles through prosperous country and good farms, and would develop not only the fishing and lumbering industries, but would encourage the construction of pulp and paper mills, and assist one of the Fraser Companies pulp mills now on that side of the Miramichi river, without rail connection.
We are handicapped by the fact that there are no railways running on that shore. If the railway was constructed there it would tend to the development of the country, and farming would be carried on more extensively. I think that part of the country is more closely inhabited than any part of Canada. Many

Acadians are in there and doing wonderful work in farming. They are developing the country, and if encouragement is extended, many more will come in, take up land, and make New Bunswdck a desirable province from the farming standpoint.
There is a great opportunity for the extension of the pulp industry in that section, as power will be brought from Grand	Falls in large quantities,	and
great developments will be made possible. We would have another pulp mill and possibly paper mills, as well as hardwood mills, in that section that would contribute very largely to the paying possibilities of that railroad. There is along the line that railway would cover, a pulp mill built by the Fraser Companies Limited one of the most energetic and progressive concerns that we have in New Brunswick, and one which has done a great deal for 'the industrial advancement of our province. This pulp mill is situated on the opposite side of the Miramichi river from Chatham, away from railway facilities. They would be wonderfully assisted and their industry would possibly be increased to a great extent if they were able to bring in their coal and ship out their manufactured product by a railway passing by their door. I would draw the attention of the government to this, because I think it is worthy of their consideration. I hope, in bringing in their branch line legislation for this year, they will not forget to put in a substantial item to make at least a beginning of the extension of that line of railway from Tracadie along towards Newcastle, to be finished and carried forward as an extension and loop of the Canadian National Railways.
We have our grievances and our burdens as hon. members can see. We are Canadians and shall remain Canadians, but let it not be forgotten that we are an important part of this great Dominion-the eastern door. As we enter this building, we see engraven on stone that it may ever be kept in mind:
The wholesome sea is at her gates,
Her gates both east and west.
We are that eastern gate. Canada needs both her gates and Canada will develop and be great as she passes the products of this country through her gates to distant lands.
Let us get together and solve our difficulties, harmoniously working together east and west and intervening parts, and let us make this Canada of ours what the Great Creator really intended when He placed us here and gave us such wonderful natural advantages-the greatest country in the world

Mr. Speaker, the budget has been presented much earlier this session than is the general custom. It may be that this accounts for the fact that some long overdue legislation has not yet been presented to the House.
The need for re-valuation of lands taken up under the Soidier Settlement Act wa3 clearly demonstrated to the government in the committee which investigated this question last session. The Soldier Settlement Board began its operations in the province of Manitoba,- and naturally the abuses, which crept into the locating of soldier settlers, were, perhaps, more pronounced in that province. I desire to bring to the attention of this House the government's obligation in this matter. When the returned soldier applied to the Soldier Settlement Board for a farm, he was shown a list of farms with descriptions and prices. These farms had been inspected by supposedly expert valuators, employed by the board for that purpose. If the valuator did not approve the price asked for the farm, he would naturally not allow it to be listed in the office of the board. The inclusion of a farm in the list shown to the applicant was in the nature of a guarantee that the list price represented the actual value of the land. Under this plan many returned men were settled on lands totally unfit for farming, and the board finally realized the situation which had developed and made a thorough house-cleaning after about two years operation. If there was nothing wrong with the valuation, there would have been no necessity for the clean-up which took place at that time. By their action the board admitted that there was something wrong with the valuation that had been carried on in certain districts in Manitoba.
The board is to be commended for its action, but it did not go far enough. What about the soldier settler who was the victim in these cases? Except for the amendments of 1922 which gave him more time in which to meet his payments, nothing has been done to lighten his burden of debt, which in many cases was improperly placed upon him. The board prevented a recurrence. of the trouble, but it made no restitution for the wrongs already done. These facts must be considered together with the serious depression which the policy of deflation brought upon agriculture, and a re-valuation of lands, particularly in districts most affected by the early administration of the act, is imperative at this time, the alternative being more abandoned and untaxa-ble lands and more men moving to the cities to increase the unemployment prob-107i
lem. I trust that the government being in possession of all the facts, will bring down the legislation necessary to meet this situation.
A somewhat similar situation has arisen among certain settlers in various parts of western Canada. In the constituency of Selkirk, which I have the honour to represent, quite a number of Scandinavians and Ruthen-ians were settled some years ago on land which should never have been thrown open for homestead entry. These lands consist of stony ridiges, stony scrub land with a very shallow loam on a gravelly subsoil.. The settlers on these lands have eked out an existence as long as there was cordiwood available. Wood is getting scarce now, and the crop failure this year, which left them without even potatoes for their own use, has resulted in great hardship and destitution. The present condition of some of these people is serious, and I would suggest that, where they are settled on manifestly unsuitable land, they be granted the right to homestead again in a better district,

Yes, but my hon. friend has misunderstood me. In the latter part of my remarks perhaps I did not make it clear, but I was referring to actual homesteaders, not to soldier settlers.
Turning to the arguments advanced in this discussion, the protectionists in this House have become greatly concerned over the working-man, and no doubt the full dinner pail will be their election .cry. I do not think that the workers of Canada can be deceived m that way. They cannot be taxed into prosperity. Any system which places greater burdens of taxation upon a man with a family than upon a bachelor will never appeal seriously to the Canadian workman. Protection increases the cost of living, and therefore decreases the purchasing power of the consumer, lessens the worker's demand for his own product and at the same time places him under a handicap when competing with workmen in other countries. One might well ask of those vho claim that protection protects labor: Why not exclude all who would compete against them in the labour market? But, very properly, these advocates of protection are in favor of an aggressive immigration policy. The value of their professions of concern for the interests of Canadian labour may be better judged by their actions. I would like to point out that those who stand for the protection of Canadian workmen embrace every oppor-
The Budget-Mr. Bancroft

tunity to employ workmen of other nationalities when such employment means increased profits.
Has protection protected Canadian labour in the case of the canneries on the Pacific coast? If my memory serves me right, drastic regulations have had to be invoked1 to force the canners of British Columbia to employ even a small percentage of Canadian labour. The largest Canadian steamship companies operate under British instead of Canadian registry. They register in Great Britain to enable them to employ British seamen to compete with Canadian seamen. Canadian steamship companies operating between Vancouver and the Orient mam their boats with coolies hired in China. The British Empire Steel Company operating boats between Montreal, Sydney, Halifax and St. John, and enjoying the fullest possible protection under the Canadian coastal navigation laws, brought in 105 Chinese coolies to replace Canadian seamen on their boats. In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, there can be no security for Canadian workmen until the purchasing power of this country is restored and until our industries 'are established ion a natural rather than an artificial basis.
In discussing the budget last year I pointed out that the reduction of the sales tax offered less relief for the taxpayers than would an equal reduction of revenue from the customs tariff. If the $20,000,000 taken off the sales tax had been taken off the tariff a very much larger amount would have been saved to the consumers, since the hidden bonuses paid to the protected industries would have been proportionately lessened. A very large increase of purchasing power would have resulted and much of the existing depression in eastern industries might have been avoided.
In the same discussion, the government will recollect, we on this side of the House asked that there should be something in the nature of an appeal provided which would enable any importer who felt that the administration of the dumping clause was unjust to obtain a decision of the facts in the particular case by an impartial tribunal. My recollection is that the government expressed itself sympathetically to the proposal, but nothing has been done.

I knew there was something wrong about it. This session we have had a proposal to widen the scope and application of the dumping clause. This proposal has now been withdrawn, but its withdrawal does not remove the original objection urged in this section of the House to the existence of the anti-dumping clause nor the suspicion that it is utilized to the injury of Canadian consumers. We welcome the change in the government's proposals, remarkable at it may be that so important a feature of the budget to which the government may be assumed to have given serious consideration before bringing the budget down should be destroyed by its sponsors so soon after its introduction. The history of the anti-dumping clause is illuminating as showing the necessity for unremitting vigilance to prevent encroachments by the protected interests. Clause 6 of the Customs Act of 1907 permitted the special duty to 'be levied when the actual selling price to an importer was less than the fair market value in the country of origin. This was amended in 1914 to allow a differential of five per cent between these two prices before the dumping duty was applied. Last year this differential was abolished by order in council but as the result of strong protest was again restored. This year's amendment would again have abolished the differential and would have given the Minister of Customs and his officials power to say what the value of any commodity imported would be for customs entry. The only definition we have of value for customs entry is that given by the minister in the amendment of 1922 relating to imports of natural products. The minister said it might be the price of the goods on the Canadian market. The old law placed a limit beyond which the minister could not go; that was, the fair market value in the country of origin. Had the amendment proposed in this budget carried the Minister of Customs would have had the power to increase protection to where it would become a practical embargo against the importation of goods, irrespective of the tariff schedule passed by this House. It is noteworthy also that goods which are listed in the tariff schedule as being free of customs duty, such as binder twine, cream

I want to say to the right hon. gentleman that the low tariff forces in this country will get together, that every attempt to increase protection drives them together and assists very materially in bringing about a clear cut division between the low tariff advocates and the protectionists.
