Mr. Speaker, with hon. members who have preceded me, I desire to express my regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is unable to be in his place. I hoped he would have recovered long ere this.
I congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the splendid showing he has been able to make under rather adverse circumstances. There can be no doubt that not Canada alone has passed through a rather serious depression dtiring 1924, but also our neighbours to the south, in fact the whole world. It is a favourite pastime of my hon. friends opposite to dilate on the fact that Canada is suffering from a condition which they would have us believe is not also present in the United States. True, they admit that in Great Britain and on the continent difficulties have been encountered by the governments of the day, that unemployment is rampant, but they never state that a similar condition of affairs exists across the line. Of course, their panacea for all our troubles is an increase of tariff.
Before dealing with that matter I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on his address delivered
this afternoon. Naturally it represents his standpoint. I must take issue with him for neglecting to ascertain that exactly the same system of accounting which is in existence today, and which he criticized so severely, has obtained for a number of years. I have taken the trouble to interview the Deputy Minister of) Finance with) respect to this system, for I confess that I shared with some other members the feeling that perhaps the country's accounts could be presented to the House in a somewhat more intelligible form. I am bound to say in fairness to him and to the officials of his department that I believe they are making a fair presentation of the facts respecting the country's accounts just as they stand in the books. Furthermore, that gentleman informs me that no Minister of Finance under whom he has acted has ever interfered with him in the slightest in the manner of making up these accounts, which he compiles in the same way every year, giving a true record of the receipts and expenditures for the fiscal year. Our public debt at the end of the last fiscal year was $2,417,734,274.88; the ordinary revenues-estimated for the current year-and apparently we have no dispute about this-will amount to $344,000,000; our consolidated fund expenses will amount to $319,700,000; our capital charges on public works-marine, railways and canals -will be $18,077,000; the special account mentioned by the Acting Minister of Finance is $4,400,000; leaving a favourable balance on the year's operations of $1,823,000. Now, if we entirely separate our railway accounting from the general accounting of the government, we have no difficulty in arriving at the result. I think we are agreed that there can be no difference of opinion about the accounts so far, but apparently there is a very considerable divergence of view when we come to our railway accounting and its application. I am not going to find any particular fault with the system adopted by our predecessors in office, but simply1 offer am explanation which I think will help to clarify the situation to some extent.
Treating our ra'Hvay accounting entirely apart from the general accounting of the country, we find that up to 1920 bonds were issued to and notes taken from the railway companies to the extent of $272,000,000. Upon that occasion the then Minister of Finance, the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) adopted a different system-I presume because the railway companies were unable to pay the interest charges on those advances-and while he charged the loans to the public debt, and
1676	COMMON'S
The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Argenteuil)
increased it accordingly, he treated them as non-active. His policy has been pursued ever since.
In 1921 that was the policy pursued. In 1922 that was the policy pursued except with this difference; in that year, as explained in the speech of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), the sum of $56,000,000 odd was received from loans made to the Imperial authorities for war purposes, and not being in a position to liquidate the bonds that were maturing, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), instead of placing that sum- in a trust account to reduce the public debt, decided in view of the fact that he had to provide for the railways that year the sum of $80,000,000 odd that it would be better for him to advance the cash received from these loans to the Imperial government than to float new loans and to turn over the proceeds to the railways, as had been done in previous years. Therein lies the difference.
Again, in 1923, because of the peculiar provisions of the act, which permitted the government to loan by way of cash or by guaranteeing bonds, the government again floated a loan, partly guaranteed securities, and partly cash to carry the railways that year, and $24,000,000 was carried in that way from the cash account of the country.
In 1924 we provided $18,000,000 odd of cash in loans to the railway. Had it not been for the fact that in 1922 the whole of the railway obligation was taken care of by cash, and by receipts from loans which had been gathered not from the taxpayers of this country, but from the Imperial government, no difficulty would have been experienced in understanding the situation thoroughly. The difficulty comes about in having obligations, partly cash, and partly guaranteed loans.
Bear in mind also one other class of security that perhaps makes it somewhat confusing, That is the securities issued for the purchase of equipment. In that case the government does not guarantee. The security is taken upon the equipment itself, and there again you have another more or less special account. So you have three systems in vogue in the railway accounting: one of guaranteeing bonds by the government, another the issuing of cash, and the third the issuing of bonds by the railways for the purchase of equipment, the bonds not being always guaranteed, the security usually being taken upon the equipment.
All told we had accumulated in this way up to the end of last year in loans to the railways the sum of $582,000,000. That is the amount that has gone into the railways, and

upon that we have delayed interest of $131,000,000. The total amount required annually for the payment of government loans and loans to the public, overhead and fixed charges, is $62,000,000 odd. Nearly $30,000,000 of these fixed charges is due the government, and of course not paid. Unfortunately, the railway company is not able out of its earnings to take care of even the fixed charges that are due to the public.

Another

He did not mention that last year there was a reduction in the sales tax estimated at almost twenty-four million dollars. We anticipated that in the beginning of the year. I am willing to admit a certain reduction, but I want to point out clearly that that did not come about because of the reduction in the tariff, nor because we happened to have a moderate tariff in Canada, as against the highly protective tariff in the United States which my hon. friends are always holding up as an example to be emulated by the Canadian people. The lessened taxation accounts in a very large measure for the reduction. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) both regret the fact of there being no reduction in taxation. Their amendtaents state that specifically. I want to point out to those hon. gentlemen that we have made a very material reduction in taxation all along the line, and that to-day we are collecting less revenue than was collected in 1920.
I wish to deal with this matter for a moment or two. The uncontrollable and the controllable expenditure of the country was as follows:

We are reducing just as fast as we can. These are mostly war expenditures-not all of them, but a very large proportion-and it may be a just and equitable criticism for my hon. friend to say that we are spending too much money as a result of the aftermath of the war and that we are not curtailing quickly enough in our expenditure. I am not going to say as to that. Perhaps the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment (Mr. Beland) could answer that question very much better than I could, but I say that this sum is made up of what is uncontrollable expenditure, and it is made up by the same gentleman who makes up the public accounts of the country and who has been making them up for the past seven or eight years to the knowledge of hon. gentlemen in this House. They are exactly the same items that are contained in the expenditures of 1914 or 1911 that I have quoted for the information of the House. The charge that we have not reduced taxation and that we are not running the country economically is surely answered in its entirety when I say that we are running the country more cheaply, as far as controllable expenditure is concerned, than the government did in 1914, the year previous to the war. No sensible or sane man will argue that the country has not grown and that the public service of the country does not require more money to run it. That statement cannot be successfully controverted and I hope the controllable expenditure will continue to rise. Indeed I am bound to say that I believe it would lend encouragement to the people were the government to spend

We have cut and cut to the core, and I want it to go out to the country that that is what the government has done and is going to do all the time. We may be a moribund government; we may be guilty of misstatements, as the hon. member said this afternoon, but these are uncontrovertible facts that I commend to his attention and to that of hon. gentlemen opposite when they are criticizing this government in its administration of the country.

Now 1 mention this because it has a bearing on what hon. gentlemen opposite are always preaching, that is, that the panacea for all our ills is increased protection with a view to increasing manufactures and so providing employment. Well, protection did not bring about any such result 'at that time, and I know of no country in the world, nor can any hon. gentlemen opposite point to one, where protection can be carried on to better advantage than in the United States. The problem we are concerned with is how we can manage our own affairs in the best interests of the Canadian people, let them raise the tariff as high as they please in the United States. But my hon. friend will not cure the difficulty. If that is his solution for preventing the Americans taking a mortgage on this country, then I fear that in the way he stated it this afternoon, it will not be effective to any very appreciable degree at all events. Do we not want American investments in Canada? If we are going to succeed, shall we not require millions of dollars to develop our natural resources? They cannot be allowed to lie undeveloped. The money must come from somewhere, and I would be pleased, indeed delighted, if all of it were to come from the Old Land, but I do not believe we can expect this, although I think we may expect English capital in increasing volume. Needless to say, we cannot expect it at the rate we hope if we are to succeed in the development of our resources. Then if this argument for protection is not going to help us in that direction, I fail to see how it will help at all. I am not going to raise any wail about the agriculturists of Canada. I think in days gone by hon. gentlemen opposite have said some rather harsh things about conditions in the Dominion and the inactivity of this government because we did not reduce the tariff to help 50 per cent of our population engaged on the farms. Undoubtedly Canada is a desperately hard country to govern. I think everyone who has had a turn at the job will admit that. In central Canada we have a group of men who are engaged very largely in manufacturing, or at least who make the most noise about it and say, " We want protection." Not protection in a moderate degree, not protection that will put them on an equality, as they fondly remark, with their fellows in other countries, but protection that will give them special privileges. That is the demand throughout this part of the Dominion. But I cannot believe that their view is shared by a very large proportion of the people in eastern Canada. Then in the Maritimes the people are very much in the same position as they are in western Canada. My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Snowball) quoted this afternoon a statement made by an ex-minister, Mr. McCurdy, who sat with the right hon. leader of the opposition in the government over which he had the honour to preside, that he did not believe a policy of protection was in the best interests of the people of Canada. So I think I am
safe in assuming that the people of the Maritime provinces are a unit with the people of western Canada in desiring that we have at least only a moderate tariff for the benefit of Canadian industries.
It has been stated, Mr. Speaker, that I am an out-and-out free trader. If I ever entertained that idea I had to give it up during the war. I well realize that we cannot have free trade in Canada, I think I have stated that on more than one occasion since I came to this House, but I have been depicted as one member of this government who would wish to destroy every vestige of the tariff in order to bring about free trade. I never made any such statement; I do not make it now; but I most emphatically say I do not believe that adequate protection, or high protection, that our hon. friends are so fond of demanding, is either necessary or in the best interests of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I think I have said sufficient to indicate that the country is not in such a deplorable condition as hon. gentlemen opposite would have us believe. I think I have said sufficient to show that the accounting of the country is safe in the hands of the Acting Minister of Finance, and that the accounting reflects the true condition of the railway situation in Canada. I think I have said enough to convince even hon. gentlemen opposite that the panacea for all our ills, be they small or great, is not increased protection.
Now imay I speak for a moment on the outlook for the future? We have to remember our situation, our climatic conditions our location upon the North American continent, with a rather small area northward, and a tremendous area east and west, with a population somewhat diverse, and with, I will admit, some difficulties, owing to the fact that markets have been shut off by our neighbours to the south; but I do not admit for a single moment that higher protection would be the cure for that difficulty. We have vast undeveloped natural resources, particularly of coal, and I want to say a word or two on that, because hon. gentlemen are anxious to know what we are going to do about the coal situation.
A great deal has been said about a national coal policy for Canada. For the last couple of years the officers of my department have been devoting some attention to the coal situation in Canada, and if I may be permitted to take a moment or two, I should like to mention a survey that we made last year in connection with coal mining operations in the United States as they affect Canada. WTe have an abundance of coal, but unfortunately it is situated in the extreme east, in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and in the far west, in western Alberta and British Columbia. Throughout the whole area of central Canada no discoveries of coal have been made up to date, and from year to year we have to import in the neighbourhood of twenty-two or twenty-three million tons of coal from the United States. It has been said that in a cold country coal is just as vital to the residents as bread. Having that in mind we thought the first problem to be tackled was that of domestic fuel. I find that year by year we import into Canada about 4,000,000 tons of domestic coal. This hard coal, or anthracite coal, comes into the country as far west as Winnipeg and even into the Maritime provinces. The quantity imported into the Maritime provinces is very small it is true, and the bulk of the imports go into the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Last year we voted a sum of money for the purpose of assisting in the transportation of domestic coal from the Maritime provinces and western Canada. I want to say frankly that I think something should be done, and can be done to reduce that production cost in Canada; it will mean a very extended market for the coal industry in this country. But coming to the situation as it exists, I said something about hoping to establish coking industries in the east-at Montreal, at Quebec, and at other large cities-in order that we might supplant as far as possible the importations of anthracite into the area in question by the substitution of the slack coal of Nova Scotia, which can be coked and makes a high grade product. That is what we hope to accomplish and thereby give to the Nova Scotia mines-in addition to the advantages they will otherwise get-an annual consumption in Canada of at least one and a half millions tons of a product that up to the moment has to go upon the dump very largely.
You will note Mr. Speaker, that there has been coming into Canada since 1921 particularly, an increased quantity of slack coal which is sold at the pit mouth in the United States for about $1 a ton and which makes a very cheap commodity and one which can be landed in" Canada at an exceptionally low rate. There have been developments in the grates used in industry for the purpose of burning slack, roller grates having been placed in many of the manufacturing establishments, and no doubt fuel costs have been very largely met by this process. But we have discovered that there has been a tremendous increase in the consumption of daek, and one of the difficulties we have experienced at the border is that of preventing the entry into Ontario and Quebec markets of large quantities of slack that should be listed as run of mine. Consequently we have had a considerable loss of duty on importations of this product, so much so that this coal has penetrated into Winnipeg and westward and taken from the Alberta mines the bituminous markets that formerly at least for a few years, they held. I am bound to say that it has had a rather demoralizing effect both east and west upon the coal fields of Nova Scotia and the coal fields of Alberta. I hope that the increase of this duty will cure this situation and that we will not be troubled at least in the future with the difficulty of ascertaining whether or not a large quantity of this commodity has been coming into Canada paying only fourteen cents duty when it should have paid fifty-three. Three cents is not much of a reduction, but remember the 108i
Canadian railways that purchase their coal in the United States will benefit to an extent. Furthermore I wish to say that very careful investigation was made with respect to this particular increase and its effect upon the manufacturers, and I think I can assure the House that not one-fifth of one per cent will be added to the overhead by the increased duty even upon manufacturing industries using slack coal in its entirety. So that no particular harm will be done, but it will increase the market for the coal fields east and west, and thereby assist an industry which has been having a rather difficult time. It is true the duties are not always responsible for these difficulties. Strikes have been prevalent on these properties. We had a strike in Alberta during the whole of last summer and a strike is in process in Nova Scotia at the present time, and these strikes have a very demoralizing effect upon the coal industry. But I say-and I want to emphasize the point-that in some way or other there must be a reduction in mining costs both east and west in order that the operators may place their commodity on the market at a more reasonable price than they have been able to do in the past, I do not think they can complain very much about the railway rates.

Something has been said about the water powers and I should have mentioned the question. My horn friend from Vancouver Centre referred to that subject this afternoon. He said the imposition of an export tax on electric power meant but one thing in his estimation, namely that we intended to encourage the export of power. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, in my department, and so far as I am concerned as a member of this government, I have never heard anything of the kind; rather to the contrary. There is a law upon the statute book at the moment authorizing us to issue licenses for only one year, and so far as I can ascertain that is all that the government intend to do in that direction. Whatever their intention may be, as a member of the government I have not heard of any change of policy. What I do say is that notwithstanding the fact that we have only developed to the extent of three million odd horsepower out of a possible development of forty-one million horsepower, I think it is good business to keep the cheap power in Canada for the development of Canadian industry, and I see no objection, and my hon. friend opposite sees no objection, to the imposition of an export duty. They all have their peak loads and that is what they are exporting at the present moment to a large degree. I see my hon. friend opposite shaking his head. I believe the Hydro Electric Commission at Niagara have a long contract for the export of power, but I do not know of any other case. I was making inquiry as to that, and so far as I know there is only the one contract. I think that as one means of

assisting the development of power we are entitled to an export tax on the power which goes out, to assist in the development of industries which will come into competition with our own. So that we have tremendous possibilities for developing this power, and there too do we not need the capital for Canada? We will find the capital in Canada for the development. We can point with some pride to the fact that eighty per cent of the debt of Canada is owed to the people of Canada, and the interest goes to the people of Canada. But we will need that money and' additional millions of money for the development of water power alone in Canada, for the development of agriculture and for the development of our mining and fishing industries.
On the authority of the best mining authorities in Canada the statement is made that we are only at the beginning of things so far as mining is concerned, that there are immense possibilities in mining, that the development in the next few years will be phenomenal, that the eyes of the world are turned towards Canada, and that the 'increase in mining activities in Ontario and Quebec alone has been unprecedented.
So far as fishing is concerned, in my own province and in Saskatchewan and in the northern waters of Manitoba nothing has been done in the way of fishing development.

My hon. friend is thinking of lake Manitoba. We are talking now of the country away beyond that. Hudson bay is teeming with fish, and what has been done there for the development of the fisheries? I point to these things with a spirit of optimism, in the hope that this gloomy foreboding with respect to the future of Canada is rapidly nearing cessation. Does it look as though we had reached the end of our tether? We are overbuilt in railways. That is quite true, but we have the necessary natural ressources to warrant the building of every one of these railways. All we need is the people to come in and assist us in developing. That is what is required in Canada.
Referring to our forest resources, perhaps we cannot be so optimistic, but I want to say that we must change the situation with respect to the destructive forces as they affect our forestry situation in Canada, in order that we may catch up with the depletion of the forests; in other words that we must grow annually as much as we cut. I should like to undertake, if it is at all possible, the establishment, in my hon. friend's province of Manitoba, of a plant that will manufacture

The Budget-Mr. Senn
*pulp and that will be under restriction to cut in such a way that after they have cut over the territory, they can begin again where they started and have a sufficient growth to carry on for an unlimited time in a forest that will be set aside for that purpose.
These are some of the facts that I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members. I have spoken at greater length than I intended. I have tried to point out to hon. gentlemen opposite that the picture they have painted is not the picture that should be painted of Canadian industry or agriculture, but rather that we in Canada are suffering only in common with the United States, Great Britain and the continent; that we are going through exactly the same experience. I wish to point out the fallacy that hon. gentlemen hold up to this House and the country, that a change in the tariff, high protection, will be the panacea and cure for all our ills. Upon that statement I rest content, leaving it to the judgment of the country and of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to state very briefly my reasons for participating in this debate on the budget proposals which have been brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). May I add my congratulations to those that have already been extended to him on the able and concise way in which he delivered his address to the House? I cannot, however, extend my congratulations any further. I am afraid that the government- have failed to gauge public opinion correctly and to realize the needs of the country respecting economy and tariff adjustments. These proposals which are before the House at the present time are certainly not affording relief to industry which has been suffering from high taxation and which requires the help of protection. On the other hand, the statement made by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) the other night proved clearly that those who are looking for further reductions in the tariff are not satisfied either. The unfortunate part of the whole situation is this, that the people of Canada look in vain for any measure of relief for the unfavourable conditions under which they are labouring, conditions which have, in a large measure, been brought about by the ineffective policy of the present government.
I listened with a good deal of attention and interest to the address just delivered by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). He made a very serious attempt to prove that
there is no cause for alarm and that Canada is prosperous, at least to a certain extent. But he will have a good deal of trouble in convincing the people of Canada of that. Wherever you go you will hear the people asking: What is the matter with Canada anyway? Why are we not prosperous? Why is there so much unemployment and hard times? It cannot avail for the government to shut their eyes to this situation and to sit quietly by without attempting to do anything to relieve it. There are plenty of indications of the lack of prosperity and of hard times. Let me indicate to the House a few which are apparent to everyone and about which there can be very little dispute. There has been enough talk in this House of unemployment to convince everyone that there is a certain amount of unemployment, altogether too much of it, in the country. Again, there has been a good deal of talk already in this session in regard to emigration. Everybody will admit that the number of people who are leaving the country is alarming. Again, we have closed factories, running up into the hundreds, and even into the thousands. We have business failures; we have vacant houses; we have railway deficits; we have decreased revenue such as was spoken of by the Acting Minister of Finance. By no means the least alarming of all these conditions is the lack of confidence which is being displayed by industry, and no amount of talk on the part of members of the government, no amount of statistics such as were given to the House by the Prime Ministei during his speech on the Address, will serve to convince the people that Canada is in a prosperous condition. The people who have these conditions constantly before them will be led to contrast the statement of Liberal policy which is outlined in the budget address with the progressive and constructive policy embodied in the resolution that stands on the order paper in the name of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). That resolution specifies the urgent need for immediate tariff revision, and I am one of those who believes that the protective principle should be applied in any such revision. Customs duties which were adequate twenty years ago are not so to-day. I do not believe in a little dabbling here and there with the tariff, raising the duty a little on coal, making the duty a little lower on some other commodity and so on. That is not what should be done at all. We should have a scientific revision of the whole schedule of tariff rates. When I speak about a revision of tariff rates, I do not mean that in every case the revision should be in an upward
The Budget-Mr. Senn

direction. There are some instances in which the revision might be downward and yet afford the necessary protection to allow those industries to exist.
Speaking however, about downward revision of the tariff, one cannot help wondering at the attitude of hon. members to the left of us this session. During the three sessions of parliament which have preceded this one, they made constant and effective attempts towards tariff reduction, and the government were compelled to accede to their demands because they needed Progressive support. But since the beginning of this session I have wondered why the Progressive party have not urged for any further tariff reduction and why they did not take a greater part in the debate on the Address. If they had made those demands during the debate on the Address, I am convinced the government would have been forced to concede them some further tariff reductions. It would appear, however, that they accepted the mandate of the Prime Minister, when he spoke in Toronto, that there would be no further tariff reductions this session. They seem to be making a gesture in the other direction at the present time, but the meekness with which they accepted that mandate would serve to convey to the House one of two things, either that their attitude on the tariff question is changing, or that there is some kind of an understanding between the two parties.
It is true that there have been one or two free-trade speeches from members of the Progressive group during this session. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) made a free-trade speech during the debate on the Address. Amongst other things he mentioned the inferior quality of goods that were produced by a certain glass company situated in Hamilton that has had to go out of business. He also said that other industries were demanding higher protection because they were lying down on the quality of their goods. I wonder if he meant to convey to the House the impression that the United Farmers of Quebec, in their demand for protection for certain of their commodities, are producing an inferior quality of farm products. I have before me the report of the annual meeting of the Ontario Vegetable Growers' Association at which there was passed a resolution asking for higher protection on vegetables and some other farm commodities. I wonder if the hon. gentleman meant to suggest that they were lying down on the quality of their product. Then we have the woollen and knitted goods industry which has suffered severely as a result of the increase in the British preference and

because of the French treaty. I want to deny most emphatically the imputation that the product of our woollen and knitted goods factories is inferior to the product of mills of a similar character elsewhere. It is true they dc need protection but they need it for an entirely different reason which I shall attempt to make clear to the House later on.
I want to deal for a few moments with the need of protection, from two standpoints particularly, first from the standpoint of agriculture, and secondly from the standpoint of the woollen and knitted goods industry which I believe is more closely allied to agriculture than any other industry, because of the fact that its raw material is an agricultural product. If proof is required of -the urgent need of tariff revision in agricultural products it should only be necessary to compare the Canadian tariff schedule wdth that of the United States. A year or two ago I made a comparison in the House in that very respect showing clearly that on almost every line of farm products the American commodities can enter this country at a much lower rate than is enjoyed by Canadian goods going into the United States. I have heard different members of the House, particularly to my left and sometimes across the way, make the statement that the farmer cannot be protected. I think my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) made that statement the other night. I cannot agree with that contention at all.
I believe that the farmer can be benefited by a proper protective policy in two ways: First, the protective policy should be such sis to create confidence on the part of industries, which give employment to our consuming population, and by so doing help to create and maintain a large home market; secondly, if that policy is to be effective our home market must be protected from undue competition on -the part of foreign products by imposing adequate duties on all classes of farm products.
By way of illustrating my first argument let me refer to the discussion which has taken place in the House as to the number of people who have left Canada during the past three vears. No one will deny that the number is so large as to be alarming. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) proved to the satisfaction of the House the other day that a conservative estimate of the number would be approximately 600,000 people, I have with me copy of a bulletin issued by the Department of Labour, called Prioes in Canada. On page 2? of that bulletin may be found a weekly family budget. I have made from that statement a list of commodities and the prices of those commodities,

The Budget-Mr. Senn
such as are produced from Canadian farms, and I find that the average cost per person amounts to something like $1.66 per week. If these 600,000 people could have been retained in Canada by a wise protective policy they would have consumed at this rate something like $5,179,200 worth of agricultural products per year, or it would' have meant they would have consumed $130 worth of products from each of 40,000 Canadian farms. Or, to illustrate this in another way, according to official returns which I have with me, we exported last year 13,648,000 pounds of butter. If each of these people had consumed twenty-three pounds in the year, or less than one-half pound per week, we would have had no exportable surplus at all and our home market would have been sufficient to absorb all our products. During the year 1923 we exported nearly 3,000,000 dozens of eggs, while we imported practically the same amount. If these people had been kept in our own country by a wise policy of tariff protection there would have been no need to export any of our eggs. The same effect would be produced to a greater or less extent in all other classes of farm products. Turning to the other side of the question, if tariff rates on farm products were sufficient in many lines, the American product would be kept out of our markets at a time when our prices are such as to allow a measure of profit over the cost of production. This is nowhere more apparent than in the case of fresh fruits and vegetables, butter and eggs and other farm commodities. The American product comes into Canada at a time when prices are particularly high, and the result is that by the time our own product is ready for market, prices are beginning to drop and the Canadian producer gets a less price in his own market than was obtained for the imported produce. If anyone should enjoy the benefits of the best prices it is our own Canadian producer. The 1919 platform of the Liberal party had free food stuffs as one of its planks. This was intended no doubt to appeal to the consuming population of our towns and cities; but free food stuffs cannot benefit people if their earning capacity is lessened by undue competition in their own line of product.
Customs duties which were adequate on farm products twenty years ago, when the prices of those commodities were very low, are not sufficient to-day, and there is some justification for the contention that the tariff discriminates to a certain extent against the Canadian farmer. If, however, the schedule
of rates on agricultural products were thoroughly revised to assure adequate protection, I am sure that this contention would be entirely overcome.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) to-night talked about a tariff for revenue, and I think the subamendment which was moved by the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) the cither night
10 p.m. also had reference to the same thing. Now I contend that a protective tariff is also a revenue tariff and to prove that contention I will give a few figures. Let us look at what happened following reductions in the tariff made by the present government particularly in 1922-23. In 1919 our dutiable imports amounted ito $526,494,000, while the duty collected was $158,046,000. In 1924, following reductions made by the present government, our dutiable imports rose to $591,142,000, while the duty collected dropped to $124,114,000; showing that while we imported more dutiable gowfe, the revenue collected was greatly lessened. On the other hand, let us consider similar figures before and after the Fordney tariff came into effebt in the United States. In 1920, their dutiable imports totalled $1,985,865,000, while the duty collected was $325,645,000. In 1923, after the Fordney tariff had come into effect, their dutiable imports were reduced to $1,651,110,000, while the revenue collected had increased to $582,764,000, or 75 per cent. This serves to show very clearly, Mr. Speaker, that a protective tariff is also a revenue producing tariff and is the best and mod; effective way of increasing our revenue from customs duties.
A few minutes ago I said that the woollen industry was very cl/osely allied to that of agriculture. Canada is a cold country in winter, and every Canadian is interested in the production and manufacture of wool. The estimated annual consumption of wool in Canada is 70,000,000 pounds on a grease basis, or as it comes from the back Of the sheep, and that is the way in which the producer is paid for his wool. Our own product in 1924 was approximately 13.000.000 from Sheep and lambs. We exported 6,300,000 pounds, or about one-half of this, while we imported 33,000,000 pounds of woo1! on a grease basis in the form of raw wool, tops, noils, waste and yam, but we also imported 40,000,000 pounds on a grease basis in the form of woollen goods further manufactured than yam. There are about 40,000 farmers keeping Sheep in Canada, and they find it a very profitable kind1 of live stock. Anyone who follows the reports of our live stock markets will see that lambs are selling at a price that is uniform and fairly high. Out Canadian wool is also selling at a
The Budget-Mr. Senn

much better price than it formerly did. It is said that the annual consumption of wool in the world to-day is 300,000,000 pounds per annum more than pre war consumption, and yet the number of Sheep in the world is less than before the war. In a country with a climate like Canada where people must wear wool for comfort, it would seem that wool growing should appeal in a very direct way to agriculture. The tariff schedules are out of date so far as the wool tariff is concerned and were framed for conditions which no longer exist. What is required to build up the wool production of Canada for the benefit of our farmers and of the wool working industry is a scientific tariff on wool and woollen products to encourage the manufacture of wool in Canada from the raw material as it comes from the back of the ^heep through all its processes to the finished article.
Many statistics have been given in this House during the past year or two to show the precarious condition not only of the woollen industry but of the knitted goods industry as well. Owing to the great increase in the British preference in 1922-23, the importation of woollen and knitted goods has largely increased. To show the effect of the increase in the British preference, I have taken from the monthly reports of the trade of Canada, the total amount of imports of woollen and knitted goods from Great Britain for the calendar years 1921 and 1924. The amount in 1921 was $22,014,757, and in 1924 $31,430,902; or an increase of approximately 43 per cent. The import of knitted goods in 1921 from Great Britain was $2,897,072; in 1924 from the same source it was $4,369,354, an increase of a little over 50 per cent. A similar comparison may be made of importations of French woollen and knitted goods prior to the French treaty as against importations following that time. The French treaty came into effect in September 1923. For twelve months preceding that date importations from France of knitted and wollen goods amounted to $1,439,748. For the twelve months following that date, the imports were $3,246,813, or an increase of approximately 125 per cent.
This cannot help but have a decided influence upon the market for Canadian products. It is impossible for our knitting factories to pay wages such as they are paying and compete with the product of the cheap labour of Germany, France and Great Britain. sweaters, knitted of contrasting all wool yams for 95 cents. It is needless for me to say that our factories in Canada cannot begin to compete with such prices. I contend, and contend very strongly, that if the people of Canada consider it desirable to have a prosperous wool growing and wool working industry which will profitably employ a considerable number of workers to the benefit of the nation, who will consume as raw material a very large part of our own production, they will have to use the same methods as are being adopted by every other protectionist country.
I want to mention one of the budget proposals which I believe will meet with at least some measure of approval on this side of the House, and that is the provision for a tariff advisory 'board. I think the suspicion on the part of any industry that there is discrimination in the application of tariff rates would be overcome by the appointment of such a tariff board. This proposal is an admission on the part of the government that a tariff is necessary, and that it is only a matter of the amount of the custom duties that should be charged. Of course the success of .such a board will depend very largely upon its personnel; they should be men who are fair-minded enough not to allow their prejudices in favour of protection or of free trade to influence them in their decisions. If such men are appointed, I have no fear but that tariff revision will be successfully and thoroughly carried out.
It is not my intention to say anything in regard to the railway situation further than this: that transportation rates are bearing very heavily upon all classes of industry, not only in the Canadian west and in the Maritime provinces, but upon the Ontario farmer as well. I feel very strongly that the management of the Canadian National railways are spending altogether too liberally on rolling stock and equipment. If they would exercise the same economy which other lines of industry are compelled to do in these hard times, we would not be called upon to guarantee bonds to the extent of eighty million dollars a year.
In my opinion there is only one solution of our transportation problem. There will

Our friends opposite will admit having expended lavishly without due regard to economy and in many cases it has been well demonstrated that they unscrupulously allowed political friends to make huge war profits and attempted to justify it on the plea that it was "to win the war." Now, Mr. Speaker, that we have won the war, was it not a wonderful achievement in itself? It was noble patriotism to help winning the Great war; so must it be highly patriotic and worthy of Canadian citizenship to meet our war obligations.
It has been demonstrated again and again that ordinary expenditures under the present administration are well within the mark and that the heavy burden on the tax payer is very largely made up, of extraordinary expenditures which neither this government nor any other that may come for a generation, will ever be in a position to eliminate or control. It would only cumber Hansard to go into this subject in detail. Figures have been given time and again and have never been refuted. But it will be said that the time has now arrived where war taxes could be reduced. It must be remembered Mr. Speaker, that war expenditures are as much of a drain on ordinary and extraordinary revenues to-day as they were when the world's greatest conflict was at its highest pitch. It does not sound very logical to say that war charges are as much of a drain on our revenue to-day as they were when war was on. In my point of view, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that they are much more so. It is readily admitted that war expenditures were provided for by huge loans, and war taxation was resorted to for the redemption of these loans; or in other words, the whole war expenditures have been a drain on the present generation as they will be on future generations. At the end of the fiscal year of 1914 the interest charge on our debt

was 814,687,797, whereas at the end of the fiscal year of 1923, on an interest bearing debt of $2,653,867,212 we had an interest charge of $136,007,667. I have not before me an exact statement of war expenditures, but it might fairly be stated that we have to meet in round figures interest on war charges amounting to over $100,000,000. If we add to this some $34,000,000 for soldiers' pensions, we will find that the drain on our ordinary revenues on these two items alone is greater than ever, and uncontrollable. Therefore the war burden on the tax payers of Canada is as cumbersome as ever and the question is more vital then ever. It thus behooves every Canadian citizen whatever his political affiliation may be, to shoulder his part of the burden and help the Canadian nation through.
The ordinary elector will say that we have nc more war expenditures. It is true we have debts bearing huge interest, and we have to pay a large amount of soldiers' pensions; but the fact remains that during the years 1914 to 1918 inclusive, while we were struggling for the liberty of the civilized nations, this parliament resorted wholly and solely to war loans to pay war expenses. No provision was made for sinking fund and no provision was made for the conscription of wealth. Probably if there was a reason why, as an elector of this Dominion, I voted against conscription, it was solely because there was no conscription of wealth, which was a great mistake, and I believe that while huge profits and fortunes were made right and left in this country, the time was opportune to levy on the wealth of the country to pay war expenses. After all, when we sum up the situation in Canada, notwithstanding the lack >of foresight on the part of our friendis diagonally opposite when they were in power, notwithstanding the fact that they have failed to provide for the redemption of these war expenditures and notwithstanding the fact that they failed to enforce the conscription of wealth during this great conflict, I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that conditions in Canada are not at all so bad as they are sometimes represented. I believe it is a great mistake for the press of this country and for hon. members opposite, or to your immediate left, to advertise Canada as a country facing blue ruin; for after all our debt per capita is not greater than the debt of the United States. Although we have a huge debt, the main creditors of Canada are her own sons and daughters. No less than three-quarters of our debt is comprised of war loans which have been floated within Canada, and consequently we have as our creditors our own people. Surely those who have been patriotic enough to
